Moderator: 
Ladies and gentlemen, good day and welcome to the Tata Capital Q2 FY27 Media Conference 
Call. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and there will be an 
opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should you need assistance 
during the conference call, please signal an operator by pressing star then zero on touchtone 
phone. 
I now hand the conference over to Mr. Rajiv Sabharwal, Managing Director and CEO of Tata 
Capital. Thank you and over to you, sir. 
Rajiv Sabharwal:  
Thank you very much. Good evening, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Let me start with 
the macro environment. The Indian economy continues to demonstrate strong fundamentals and 
broad-based momentum despite external headwinds. GDP grew by 7.8% in the first quarter of 
FY27, supported by healthy investment activity and steady private consumption. 
Credit demand also remained resilient during the second quarter. At the same time, we remain 
watchful of inflationary pressures arising from food and energy prices, geopolitical 
developments in West Asia, and their potential implication for consumption and interest rates.  
Following the RBI's 25 basis points repo rate increase in October and the gradual recalibration 
of system liquidity, we expect funding conditions to become less accommodative. Nevertheless, 
India's growth drivers remain supportive and we continue to see an environment supportive of 
credit growth. 
Turning to our performance, consolidated AUM crossed the INR3 lakh crores milestone and 
stood at INR3,08,030 crores, growing at 26% year-on-year and 6% sequentially. If we exclude 
the motor finance business, the AUM grew by 32% year-on-year. Profit after tax stood at 
INR1,660 crores for quarter 2, increasing 51% year-on-year and 7% sequentially.  
The return on assets stood at 2.3% and excluding Motor Finance, it was 2.5%. Our ROE crossed 
14%. Asset quality remained resilient. Gross Stage 3 assets were stable at 1.9%, while the 
provision coverage ratio improved to 59%. The annualized credit cost declined to 0.9% in Q2 
over 1.0% in Q1. 
Retail and SME businesses remain central to our strategy and account for approximately 85.4% 
of the consolidated AUM, providing a diversified, granular, and resilient portfolio. 
Disbursements across our high-margin businesses grew by 40% year-on-year, while AUM 
growth increased to 14%, up from 10% in Q1, while maintaining healthy yields. 
Tata Capital Housing Finance continued its strong trajectory. The AUM at Tata Capital Housing 
Finance reached INR95,098 crores, increasing 26% year-on-year and 6% sequentially. The 
profit after tax for quarter 2 at Tata Capital Housing Finance stood at INR552 crores. Return on 
assets was 2.5% and ROE was 18%. 
We also added 23 locations across affordable and micro-housing during the quarter, further 
deepening our presence in under-penetrated markets and supporting greater portfolio 
diversification. Our branch network now is approximately 1,515 branches across 1,094 locations 
in 26 states and union territories. Supported by our digital model, we serve more than 9.2 million

customers. Our expanding distribution, digital, and data capabilities position us to deepen 
customer relationships, improve accessibility, and pursue growth opportunities efficiently.  
Our AAA rating continues to support a diversified and stable funding profile. Total borrowings 
stood at approximately INR2.61 lakh crores, while available liquidity was around INR36,400 
crores. The cost of funds marked increased marginally to 7.33% from 7.28% in the previous 
quarter. In response to the evolving interest rate environment, our ALCO approved a 20 to 25 
basis points increase in prime lending rates on the floating rate portfolio. This repricing is 
expected to support an improving NIM plus fee trajectory in quarter 4. 
Operating efficiency continued to improve with cost-to-income declining by 438 basis points 
year-on-year to now 35.3%. Consolidated AUM grew 26% year-on-year compared with a 
headcount growth of 6%, demonstrating improved productivity, scalability, and operating 
leverage across the organization. 
Technology and AI remain integral to our operating model. Today, 99% of our customers are 
digitally onboarded, 98% of retail disbursements are supported by scorecard and business rule 
engine decisioning, and 99% of our collections take place through digital channels. AI is 
increasingly embedded across customer acquisition, underwriting, operations, servicing, and 
collections. These initiatives are helping improve turnaround times, strengthen risk monitoring, 
enhance customer experience, and lower the cost of servicing. 
On the regulatory front, we continue to engage proactively with regulators and industry bodies. 
On revolving credit, FIDC, the SRO has submitted its recommendations to RBI and we are also 
evaluating alternative product structures to mitigate any potential impact. 
On insurance, the proposals are still at a draft stage and industry consultations are ongoing. It is 
therefore premature to quantify the impact. Insurance remains an important risk cover for our 
customers and integral to our underwriting, and we will have greater clarity once the final 
regulations are issued. 
To conclude, quarter 2 FY27 delivered healthy, diversified growth, resilient portfolio quality, 
and disciplined execution, supported by strong capital, diversified funding, and continued 
investment in distribution, technology, and AI. We remain focused on building a larger, stronger, 
and more resilient financial services franchise and are confident of delivering on our guidance 
and creating long-term value for our stakeholders. 
With that, we would be happy to take your questions. 
Moderator: 
Thank you very much. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. First question is 
from the line of Shrishti Sharma from ET BFSI. Please go ahead. 
Shrishti Sharma: 
Thank you. Good evening, everyone. Mr. Sabharwal, while you have already addressed the 
revolving credit part, I would request you if you could elaborate more on, what is the path you 
would be taking in case the draft norms come out the way they are. To add, your peers have 
already announced launching of some new loan variants, as a backup to the fact that revolving 
credit might be re-banned by RBI given your exposure is somewhat below 5%.

Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, first of all, we continue to engage with the regulator on this. They have also been seeking 
feedback from everyone on the nature of products, the markets which they are serving, and the 
benefits to the customers. Actually, an overdraft product is something which is very beneficial 
to the customer because it allows the customer to pay only to the extent he or she borrows. We 
looked at a lot of products which do come here and some of these products, for example, supply 
chain, loans against securities, have been in existence for more than 30 years in the industry. 
So our belief is this that the regulator is taking into consideration all of these aspects and then 
will come out with the necessary guidelines. Obviously, whatever guidelines they come out with, 
we will be fully compliant with the same. As far as we are concerned, we have looked at some 
alternate products which can help meet the needs of the customers. 
Some of these products we have already piloted in the market and the others we expect to do in 
the coming month. we do believe this will not have any significant impact over a period of time, 
but we will wait for the regulations to come in and we do believe that the regulations will take 
into account the needs of the customers as well as the necessary regulations the regulator has to 
adopt. 
Shrishti Sharma: 
But would you already be cutting down on your exposure to revolving credit since you said you 
are already piloting some of the products and more would be going live very soon. So, does that 
mean you will be cutting down the exposure even before you hear on the final norms? 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, as far as we are concerned, this is not a very large proportion of our business. we have looked 
at complying with the regulations and since it's not a very large proportion of our book, we have 
not cut down on anything. However, we have also looked at what alternate products could exist 
in the market to take care of the impact. Like for example, in personal loans or business loans, 
they are not a dominant portion of our disbursements. 
Shrishti Sharma: 
Sure. You already talked about IRDAI's distribution norms and that you cannot quantify the 
impact. while that's there, could you talk about what could be your alternative source of fee 
income in case these norms also pan out because one would really think about what the strategy 
could end up being in case something of this sort comes in the final place as well. 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
Thank you. So, we have looked at different possibilities. Number one, we look at how we can 
also look at selling the retail product in insurance. That is something which will, be good for the 
customer and also give us the relevant margins. The second point, but before that, I just want to 
say that insurance is a good product for a customer who's taking a loan. It protects him or her in 
any eventuality or loss of income or in case there are challenges on the health side. 
So, it is a good product and we always advise customers that in case they do not have, an existing 
insurance, they should look at the possibility of taking an insurance and evaluating the pros and 
cons. And we have seen so many customers who have benefited because of the fact that they 
had an insurance. 
So besides looking at retail lines of business, we do believe there is an opportunity for looking 
at how we can, mitigate the impact of this loss of income through our NIMs and fee income. So 
we will look at the possibility of using NIM, fee income as well as becoming more efficient on

cost to mitigate the impact of this. However, as I mentioned before, it is too early to talk about 
this. The engagements are on and we do hope that the final policy will be something which will 
look at not only the benefits of the person who's looking at the insurance, but also consider the 
costs involved in selling this insurance so that it balances on both sides on the distribution cost 
as well as the benefits for the customers when the final policies come out. 
Shrishti Sharma: 
Sure. Thank you.

Manju: 
Good evening. Can you hear me?

Manju: 
Yes. just wanted to ask you like what portion of your credit book would be gold and what is the 
LTV ratio and since the gold prices are falling, is there some new underwriting norms that you 
are putting in place in case, there are some delinquencies. Of course, there is no it's a stable book 
only, but in case. 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, Manju, we do not have a gold portfolio at this point of time. Our organic business should 
start in the coming month with the launch of that business. So currently, we do not have a 
portfolio in this. 
Manju: 
Okay. And I just wanted to know the revolving credit would be what portion of your total book, 
the revolving credit? 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, we had mentioned earlier that revolving credit, based on the interpretation, has a number of 
products in it. We had looked at this portfolio and when we had done an evaluation to look at 
what could be the impact in case the guidelines come as they are and what we will not be able 
to convert into a standard term loan, that impact for us was coming at 3% to 4% of our AUM. 
Manju: 
Okay. Thank you so much. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Ram Kumar from Hindu Business Line. Please 
go ahead. 
Ram Kumar: 
Hello. sir, you said that your ALCO has approved the increase in lending rates by 20 to 25 basis 
points. what is the reason for this? Is it because banks are increasing their MCLR, that is kind 
of, you are trying to pass it on? What is the outlook actually for the interest rates, lending rates 
and borrowing costs? 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
See, if you look at what the market has been talking about, the market has been saying that 
besides this the 25 basis points repo increase which has happened, there could be an increase of 
about 50 basis points in the rest of the year. But obviously, we will need to watch as things play 
out. For us, part of our liabilities are linked to repo rates and other floating rate benchmarks and 
when those benchmarks increase, then to that extent our cost of fund also goes up.

Just to give you a sense of our liabilities and assets, our floating rate liabilities are 48% of our 
total liabilities and floating rate assets are about 66% of our total assets. So structurally, we are 
very well positioned so that in case there is any increase in interest rates, we will be able to look 
at its impact on our cost of funds, change the PLR and pass on the impact because of which it 
will not in any situation be a drag on our cost. 
Ram Kumar: 
Thank you. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. The next question is from the line of Subhana Shaikh from Mint. Please go ahead. 
Subhana Shaikh: 
Hi, sir. Good evening. I wanted to ask what is the sense that you are getting on festive demand 
right now? Are you seeing, what kind of signs are you seeing on festive demand and on the rural 
side, are you seeing any stress there? Some of the lenders have flagged concerns on the rural 
side because of the drought situation. I wanted to understand what is your sense on that? 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, actually, if you look at the demand it is quite buoyant, I would say. We do get a sense from 
a few areas. First of all, in this period, you see very good two-wheeler sales and PV sales 
happening and we are clearly seeing that demand on the vehicle side, similarly on the 
commercial vehicle side also there is a strong demand. We are also seeing the impact of 
increased demand from dealers in their supply chain requirements. 
So I would say the festive demand is strong in all of these products. and obviously, we will be 
we continue to watch this, but that that is what the sense which we are getting. As far as rural 
markets are concerned, I think at this point of time, there is some bit of lag or let me say, growth 
rate which is slower in rural markets compared to the urban markets.  
However, we have very limited presence in the rural markets. We are not into tractor finance or 
agri farm loans. The only business which we have in the rural markets is microfinance, which is 
actually showing an improving asset quality trend and an improving growth rate. So we are not 
seeing any challenge on the rural side. It's also because of the fact that we have very limited 
presence in the rural markets. 
Subhana Shaikh: 
Sir, can you give a guidance on your loan growth for FY27? 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
So, we have communicated in the past that we should be growing at about 23% to 25% for the 
year as well as, over the '25 to '28 time period. So we do believe that we will be within the range 
which we have stated of 23% to 25%. 
Subhana Shaikh: 
Okay. Thank you. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will take that as the last question for today. I now hand 
the conference back to management for closing comments. Over to you, sir. 
Rajiv Sabharwal: 
Thank you very much. I think it's been an excellent quarter for us. We have seen very strong 
growth of 26%. The good part is that this growth has been across segments, whether it is housing, 
retail, SME, or corporate, it's been across all segments. Since we have created a model which

impact in quarter 2 on the cost of funds. 
Our operating leverage and our investments in digital and AI is playing out very well with cost 
to income dropping significantly. And as always, our credit quality remains the best across the 
NBFC industry and it has only got better in this quarter. So overall, an excellent quarter. We are 
looking at very positively towards growth for the rest of the year too. 
Moderator: 
Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of Tata Capitals, that concludes this conference. 
Thank you for joining us, and you may now disconnect your lines.

Ladies and gentlemen, good day and welcome to the Tata Capital Q2 FY27 Earnings Conference 
Call. As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and there will be an 
opportunity for you to ask questions after the presentation concludes. Should you need assistance 
during the conference call, please signal an operator by pressing star then zero on your touchtone 
phone. I now hand the conference over to Mr. Rajiv Sabharwal, Managing Director and CEO of

Rajiv Sabharwal: 
Thank you very much. Good evening, everyone and thank you for joining us today.  
Let me begin with a brief overview with the macroeconomic environment and its 
implication for the financial services sector.  
The Indian economy continues to demonstrate resilience, supported by domestic demand and 
investment. GDP grew by 7.8% in FY26 and sustained the same pace in Q1 FY27, reflecting 
strong economic momentum. While external uncertainties remain, the underlying growth 
outlook continues to be constructive. However, a subpar monsoon and El Nino are affecting 
food prices, while prolonged tensions in West Asia continue to exert pressure on fuel prices. 
Headline inflation has subsequently firmed up to 5.54% in September. We are monitoring these 
developments closely, particularly their implications for consumption and the interest rate 
environment. Credit momentum remained healthy through the second quarter with bank lending 
growing by over 19% in September and NBFC lending by about 16% in August. 
Activity remained broad-based, aided by sizable FCNR (B) inflows and strengthened banks 
deposit base. Growth in bank credit was also partly supported by funding substitution and 
elevated bond yields prompted corporates and NBFCs to increasingly turn to bank borrowings. 
Overall, underlying demand across the lending channels remains healthy.  
In October, the MPC raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% and shifted its stance from 
neutral to calibrated tightening amid rising inflationary pressures from food and energy prices. 
Given the evolving inflation outlook, we anticipate about 2 further rate hikes in this financial 
year.  
Liquidity conditions remain comfortable in surplus during the quarter, averaging nearly INR5 
lakh crores, supported by robust foreign currency inflows. More recently, RBI has been 
calibrating liquidity conditions through the open market sales and daily CRR maintenance 
requirements, resulting in surplus liquidity moderating to a level below INR1 lakh crores now.  
Consequently, we expect marginal funding costs to rise progressively and overall funding 
conditions to become less accommodative over the following months. Looking ahead, the RBI's 
upward revision of its FY27 growth forecast to 7.1% signals continued economic momentum, 
although the pace is expected to moderate from the first quarter.  
While geopolitical tensions in West Asia pose risks to inflation and currency stability and an 
uneven monsoon could exert pressure on food prices and rural demand, industrial activity and

festive season demand are expected to provide support and partly offset these headwinds. In this 
environment, disciplined underwriting, prudent pricing, sustained asset quality and capital-
efficient growth will remain key priorities for lenders.  
Now let me turn to the key highlights for the quarter:  
Quarter 2 FY '27 saw broad-based growth, stable asset quality and improved operating 
efficiency, reflecting disciplined execution across businesses. As of September '26, consolidated 
AUM crossed the INR3 lakh crores milestone and stood at INR3,08,030 crores, up 26% year-
on-year and 6% sequentially.  
Excluding the Motor Finance business, our AUM grew by 32% year-on-year and 7% 
sequentially. Consolidated profit after tax for the quarter stood at INR1,660 crores, registering a 
growth of 51% year-on-year and 7% sequentially. Return on assets stood at 2.3%, which 
excluding Motor Finance was 2.5%. Our ROE stood at 14%. 
As far as housing finance business is concerned: 
Tata Capital Housing Finance continued its strong performance trajectory during quarter 2 
FY'27. AUM reached INR95,098 crores, growing by 26% year-on-year and 6% sequentially. 
The portfolio remains well diversified across home loans, loans against property, construction 
finance and affordable housing.  
The affordable and micro housing portfolio within Tata Capital Housing Finance grew at 22% 
year-on-year and 5% sequentially. As we continue to deepen our presence in underpenetrated 
markets, we expect affordable housing to progressively become a larger contributor to our 
overall growth. 
During the quarter, Tata Capital Housing Finance Limited reported a profit after tax of INR552 
crores. ROA stood at 2.5% and ROE at 18.0%.  
Let me take you through our performance across our four key themes and updates on our 
digital and AI initiatives. 
On book growth: 
I'm pleased to share that Q2 saw sustained disbursement momentum across all our businesses. 
Consolidated disbursements increased by 29% year-on-year to INR51,665 crores, supported by 
healthy growth across businesses. Our consolidated AUM grew by 26% year-on-year and 6% 
sequentially. Excluding Motor Finance, AUM grew by 32% year-on-year and 7% sequentially.  
Within this, our Housing Finance segment continued its strong momentum, delivering a 26% 
year-on-year AUM growth. Retail and SME portfolio account for 85.4% of our AUM, remains 
the cornerstone of our strategy, driving sustainable growth, greater resilience and superior risk-
adjusted returns.  
Our high-margin businesses continue to show robust growth. Disbursements across these 
businesses grew by 40% year-on-year, while AUM growth increased to 14%, up from 10% in

portfolio, disciplined underwriting and robust collections infrastructure. Our portfolio remains 
diversified and granular across secured and unsecured retail, housing, SME, corporate and Motor 
Finance segments. 
We continue to closely monitor evolving macroeconomic conditions and business trends. Based 
on current indicators, we remain confident in our risk-calibrated approach and the underlying 
resilience of our asset quality.  
The third theme I would like to touch upon is our funding, capital and liquidity: 
Our AAA credit rating continues to underpin a well-diversified and stable funding profile. 
Through a disciplined ALM framework, we continue to optimize our borrowing mix while 
proactively managing liquidity and interest rate risk. Our cost of funds increased marginally 
from 7.28% in quarter 1 FY27 to 7.33% in quarter 2 FY27.  
Total borrowings stood at approximately INR2.61 lakh crores as of September 2026. The 
borrowing mix remained well diversified with bank loans accounting for approximately 39%, 
NCDs 35%, ECBs and MTNs 12% and commercial paper and WCDL at 9% and NHB 
borrowings another 3%. 
NIM declined marginally, primarily due to a modest increase in cost of funds and a slight 
moderation in yields at mortgage business. Our asset liability mix provides us flexibility to

Our fourth theme is operating leverage:  
Our cost-to-income ratio improved by 438 basis points year-on-year to 35.3% in quarter 2 FY 
'27, while cost to average assets remained well contained at 2.3%. As of September 2026, our 
on-roll employee strength stood at 31,655 with over 80% deployed in frontline sales and 
collection.  
Against year-on-year AUM growth of 26%, our headcount increased by just 6%, reflecting 
sustained gains in employee productivity and operating leverage across the organization. Our 
investments over the past few years in technology, data infrastructure, artificial intelligence and 
distribution are increasingly translating into structural improvements in productivity, operating 
efficiency and scalability.  
Looking ahead, we remain on track to deliver our medium-term guidance with operating 
leverage expected to be an important lever of further improvement in ROA.  
At Tata Capital, talking about our AI initiatives, technology is deeply embedded in our 
operating model, and AI has become a key pillar of our digital-first strategy. We are building an 
AI-first NBFC, leveraging AI across the lending value chain to enhance customer experience, 
improve productivity, strengthen risk management and create a scalable operating model for 
future growth. The focus is no longer on isolated use cases, but on enterprise-wide AI-led 
transformation.  
Our strong digital DNA is reflected in the scale of adoption across the customer life cycle. 
Today, 99% of our customers are onboarded through digital channels, 98% of retail 
disbursements are enabled through scorecard and business rule engine-based decisioning. 99% 
of collections are through digital channels and 98% of our customer queries are digitally 
addressable.

We have also built a network of over 180 digital partnerships, significantly enhancing customer 
reach and accessibility. AI is now embedded across customer acquisition, underwriting, 
operations, servicing and collections. In customer engagement, AI-generated content powers the 
majority of marketing creatives and campaign communications, while AI-led onboarding 
initiatives have enabled over 30 lakh customer interactions. 
In underwriting, our AI-powered credit intelligence and decisioning engines have processed over 
7.8 crores documents and have achieved over 95% adoption across personal loans and business 
loans underwriting, resulting in meaningful improvements in productivity and turnaround times.  
Across operations, AI-led workflows now process approximately 70% of retail applications 
driving productivity gains, faster turnaround times and lower operating costs. In servicing, AI-
